paragraph.text: “Synoptic” means “seen together.” The name fits Matthew, Mark, and Luke because they share many stories and teachings, often in a similar order or in similar words.

guides.title: How to read a Gospel comparison
guides.description: Use the storm story to practice spotting differences and reading them in context.
guides.intro: Pick one detail in a scene, trace it in each Gospel, and then see how it fits into the whole passage.

paragraphs.text: In the storm story, when does Jesus question the disciples? Matthew places his question before he rebukes the wind and the sea. In Mark and Luke, Jesus questions the disciples after the storm has subsided.

sections.title: Read each account on its own

paragraphs.text: Use Aligned groups to find related moments in the story. Try Whole passages to see how each Gospel gets from the disciples’ appeal for help to their reaction afterward. You can hide the reading notes while you look for a detail of your own.

sections.title: Follow an interpretation back to the text

paragraphs.text: Mark ends the scene with the disciples asking who Jesus is. Dale B. Martin reads their question as part of a pattern in which they keep struggling to understand Jesus. Try his reading against another scene on the water in Mark 6:45–52. What does Mark say the disciples have failed to understand there?

Questions about how the Gospels were composed draw on patterns across many passages. Goodacre looks at agreements in the Greek wording and in the order of stories. That takes the investigation beyond what you can see in any one English comparison.

links.label: Try the mustard seed and yeast exercise

guides.title: What is the Synoptic Problem?
guides.description: See why scholars propose different sources for the agreements among Matthew, Mark, and Luke.
guides.intro: How did Matthew, Mark, and Luke come to share so many details? Scholars use patterns of agreement and difference to test proposals about how the three Gospels were written.

sections.title: The patterns a hypothesis has to explain

paragraphs.text: Scholars call material found in all three Gospels the triple tradition. The storm story is one example. The double tradition is material Matthew and Luke share with each other that has no parallel in Mark. Both patterns matter because an explanation for the three-way agreements may leave the two-way agreements open.
The Two-Source and Farrer hypotheses both propose that Mark was written before Matthew and Luke, and that both authors used Mark as a source. Many scholars accept this view, called Markan priority.

In the story of John the Baptist’s death, Mark calls Herod a king. Matthew first uses Herod’s more precise title, “tetrarch,” and later calls him king too. Mark Goodacre reads the switch as a clue that Matthew revised a detail in Mark’s account and later slipped back into Mark’s wording.

The Two-Source hypothesis has the widest support among scholars, and Farrer is a leading alternative. Because both accept Markan priority, comparing them brings one question into focus. For passages shared by Matthew and Luke alone, did both use a second source, or did Luke draw directly from Matthew?

links.label: Try the exercise on who used whom

paragraphs.text: On this hypothesis, Matthew and Luke each drew on Mark and a second written source. Scholars call that proposed document Q, short for Quelle, the German word for “source.” They infer what it may have contained by comparing passages shared by Matthew and Luke that have no parallel in Mark.

A shared source would let Matthew and Luke place the same saying in different settings while writing independently. John S. Kloppenborg questions whether Luke’s direct use of Matthew explains some of those differences in arrangement.

citations.locator: Chapter 10, “The Order of the Q Material”
Abstract, on Luke’s arrangement of shared material

paragraphs.text: Austin Farrer proposed that Matthew used Mark and Luke used both Mark and Matthew. In this model, Luke’s use of Matthew explains the two-way agreements and removes the need to posit Q for that material.

Farrer argued that Luke could have chosen to break up Matthew’s long speeches and place sayings in new settings. Francis Watson proposes testing such accounts against the Q model by working through the editorial choices each explanation requires, passage by passage.

The question also arises within stories found in all three Gospels. In the mocking of Jesus, Matthew and Luke share a question that Mark’s account leaves out. Such details are called minor agreements. Farrer argued that they make sense if Luke had read Matthew.

citations.locator: pp. 60–62, on Matthew and Luke agreeing against Mark

paragraphs.text: The Griesbach or Two-Gospel hypothesis puts Matthew first, has Luke use Matthew, and has Mark draw on both. Christopher M. Tuckett traces the modern revival of this hypothesis to the work of William R. Farmer.

Could Matthew have read Luke instead? On the proposal called Matthean posteriority, Luke used Mark, and Matthew later used both Mark and Luke. Robert K. MacEwen studies stretches of identical wording and asks whether Matthew knew parts of Luke beyond their shared sayings. Mark Goodacre argues that Luke used Matthew, pointing to turns of phrase characteristic of Matthew in passages they share.

In one Marcionite-priority proposal, Matthias Klinghardt places the gospel in Marcion’s collection before canonical Luke and makes it a source in the formation of the canonical Gospels. The gospel has to be reconstructed from evidence such as quotations and reports by ancient writers. Dieter T. Roth questions how Klinghardt weighs some of that testimony.

sections.title: Try the question on a passage

paragraphs.text: Matthew puts the Lord’s Prayer in the Sermon on the Mount. Luke introduces it with a disciple’s request for instruction. Those settings are visible in the text. To ask where the prayer came from, scholars weigh that evidence alongside other parallels and consider how the prayer might have circulated. Olegs Andrejevs examines both transmission through Q and transmission through an independent tradition of worship.

guides.title: A short guide to Matthew, Mark, and Luke
guides.description: See how each Gospel opens and where a comparison passage fits in its story.
guides.intro: Read the opening of each Gospel, then follow a familiar passage back into its own setting.

paragraphs.text: Matthew opens with a genealogy that links Jesus to David and Abraham, then tells of his birth. The Lord’s Prayer appears later in the Sermon on the Mount, amid instructions about giving, prayer, and fasting.

Dale B. Martin points out that Matthew gathers much of Jesus’ teaching into five long speeches. The Sermon on the Mount is the first. Read the prayer alongside the rest of Matthew 6 and notice what kind of audience the teaching assumes.

Mark moves quickly from John baptizing in the wilderness to Jesus’ baptism and his preaching in Galilee. The storm comes later, immediately after a series of parables told by the lake. When the boat arrives at the other side, Jesus encounters a man among the tombs.

Dale B. Martin connects the disciples’ question after the storm to a wider pattern of people recognizing or failing to recognize Jesus. Try following that question from the storm to the confession in Mark 8:27–30.

citations.locator: Chapter 2, on Mark 4:41 and the disciples’ understanding

paragraphs.text: Luke opens with a preface addressed to Theophilus. The writer says that earlier accounts exist and describes his own aim in writing. Later, Luke sets the Lord’s Prayer in a longer sequence about prayer that includes a story about a friend arriving at midnight.

Loveday Alexander compares Luke’s formal opening with prefaces to ancient technical works. She sees parallels in the way Luke addresses a reader and describes his project. Read the first four verses before the story begins and notice what expectations they set.

guides.title: How can you tell who used whom?
guides.description: Mark a narrator’s interruption, then follow Herod’s title to test a claim about which Gospel was written first.
guides.intro: An unusual turn of phrase can suggest that two writers shared a text. To work out who might have read whom, try two different questions.

sections.title: Where does the narrator step in?

paragraphs.text: In all three accounts, Jesus starts to explain his authority to forgive sins. The narrator cuts in to tell us whom Jesus addresses, and then Jesus gives the command to get up. Mark Goodacre points to that shared interruption in the Greek as a clue to a written connection. The three writers have more in common here than a memory of the same saying.

citations.locator: p. 180, on Matthew 9:6, Mark 2:10–11 and Luke 5:24

paragraphs.text: A tetrarch was a regional ruler. Goodacre suggests that Matthew began by giving Herod his more precise title, then slipped back into the wording of Mark’s story. Goodacre calls this kind of pattern “editorial fatigue.” On that reading, Mark supplies a reason for Matthew’s change of title halfway through the scene.

citations.locator: pp. 46–47, on Herod’s title and his grief

links.label: Read the accounts of John’s death

sections.title: Which question did each clue answer?

paragraphs.text: The interruption makes a case for shared writing. The change of title gives Goodacre a reason to argue that Matthew used Mark specifically. Both the Two-Source and Farrer hypotheses can accept that direction. They part company over how Matthew and Luke came to share material outside Mark. Try that question on two short parables.

guides.title: Where does the story come in each Gospel?
guides.description: Trace the baptism, a healing and the hometown synagogue through three Gospel sequences.
guides.intro: Choose a scene to follow it across Matthew, Mark, and Luke. Follow each Gospel’s sequence to see what its readers have already encountered.

paragraphs.text: In Matthew and Mark, readers have already seen Jesus forgive and heal the paralyzed man when his hometown questions him. In Luke, readers encounter the hometown synagogue first. The map follows the order of these selected scenes in each book.

sections.title: What do you expect Jesus to do next?

paragraphs.text: In Luke’s synagogue scene, Jesus reads about bringing good news to the poor and release to captives, then says the scripture is being fulfilled. Joel B. Green reads the scene as an introduction to Jesus’ mission. When the paralyzed man is brought to Jesus one chapter later, how does that earlier promise shape your reading of the healing?

guides.title: The Lord’s Prayer in two copies of Luke
guides.description: Switch between the opening words in two Greek manuscripts of Luke 11:2 and explore how the prayer circulated.
guides.intro: Two people reading Luke could begin the same prayer with different words. Compare the opening address preserved in two handwritten copies.

paragraphs.text: Holger Strutwolf identifies the short address in Papyrus 75 and the longer one in Codex Alexandrinus. He understands the longer reading as an instance of copying that brought Luke closer to the familiar wording of Matthew 6:9. Comparing copies of one Gospel lets us see variation within its own history.

citations.locator: pp. 25–27, on the address and petitions in Luke 11

sections.title: Could worship have shaped the prayer?

paragraphs.text: The Didache, an early Christian teaching text, gives a version of the prayer close to Matthew’s and tells readers to use it three times a day. That instruction is direct evidence that a community was taught to pray these words regularly.

How did the prayer reach Matthew and Luke in the first place? Olegs Andrejevs examines a proposed tradition of worship alongside the possibility that both writers used Q. A copy of Luke can tell us how someone wrote the prayer out. Reconstructing what the Gospel writers heard or read calls for a separate argument.
